evidence.title: Investigating whether the turbulence model from existing small wind turbine standards is valid for rooftop sites
evidence.abstract:
The wind energy industry has developed considerably in recent years with regard to large scale wind turbines. However, the small wind turbines (SWTs) are still underdeveloped. The classification of SWTs comes under the standard IEC6140001-2. When a small wind turbine is installed in an urban environment, it is exposed to complex environmental conditions, where high “surface roughness” in urban terrain due to buildings, street furniture and various obstacles causes a highly turbulent wind. This results in fatigue developing in turbine structures and poor performance. Turbulence is therefore a very important factor in small wind turbine functioning. But, in standards, turbulence intensity is considered a constant value for all wind classes for small wind turbines.



To assess the validity of the standard normal turbulence model (NTM) for SWTs for all sites, data from an open space and an urban area are analysed and compared. The data were collected from Ostergarnsholm Island in Sweden, as the open space, and the rooftop of a Bunnings warehouse in Port Kennedy as the urban area. The results for these two areas are compared with the standard NTM.



The outcome of the comparative analysis is that the rooftop areas are subject to greater turbulence intensity than that prescribed in the standard, and the open space turbulence intensity, on the other hand, is lower than the standard. Therefore, wider investigation and research are required in order to revise and improve the standard wind classes for small wind turbines

Despite the great potential of small wind turbines to provide electric power, particularly in remote areas, many small wind turbines have short lifetimes due to technical failures or the excessive costs of numerous maintenance visits. For wind turbines to be reliable they must have in place good mechanisms to protect themselves against very high winds or sudden removal of load. Both these scenarios can lead to “over-speeding” of the turbine rotor where the rotor experiences speed excursions that exceed the rated speed of the blade manufacturer. Over-speeding can lead to blade collapse with the possibility of damage to other turbine components and people and structures in the vicinity. For small horizontal-axis wind turbines (typically in the size range 0.1 – 30 kW), passive or mechanical protection systems are often used. evidence.title: Novel methods for fatigue data editing for horizontal axis wind turbine blades
evidence.abstract:
Wind turbine blades are the most critical components of wind turbines. Full-scale blade fatigue testing is required to verify that the blades possess the strength and service life specified in the design. Unfortunately, the test must be run for a long time period. This problem led the blade testing laboratories to accelerate fatigue testing time. To achieve the objective, this thesis proposes two novel methods called STFT- and WT-based fatigue damage part extracting methods which are based on short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and wavelet transform (WT), respectively. For WT, different wavelet functions which are Morl, Meyr, Dmey, Mexh and DB30 are studied.



An aerodynamic computer code, HAWTsimulator, based on blade element momentum theory has been developed. This code is used to generate the sets of aerodynamic loads acting along the span of a ‘SERI-8 wind turbine blade’ in the range of wind speed from cut-in to cut-out. SERI-8 blades are installed on 65 kW wind turbines. Each set of aerodynamic loads is applied on the finite element model of the SERI-8 blade in structural software (ANSYS) to generate a plot of von Mises stress at the critical point on the blade versus wind speed. By relating this relationship to the wind speed data, the stress-time history at the critical point on the SERI-8 blade can be generated. It has the same sampling rate and length as the wind speed data.



A concept of applying accumulative power spectral density (AccPSD) distribution with time to identify fatigue damage events contained in the stress-time history has been introduced in this thesis. For STFT, AccPSD is the sum of power spectral density (PSD) of each frequency band at each time interval in the spectrogram. For WT, AccPSD is the sum of PSD of wavelet coefficients of each scale at each time interval in the scalogram. evidence.title: Design and construction of a simple blade pitch measurement system for small wind turbines
evidence.abstract: For small wind turbines to be reliable they must have in place good mechanisms to protect themselves against very high winds or sudden removal of load. One common protection method in small wind turbines is that of blade feathering. It is important that the blade feathering mechanism of a small wind turbine is tested before the turbine is installed in the field. This paper presents a simple system for monitoring the blade feathering of a turbine with an overall component cost that small wind turbine manufacturers can afford. The Blade Pitch Measurement System (BPMS) has been designed and constructed by the Research Institute of Sustainable Energy (RISE) and aids small wind turbine manufacturers in testing and optimising the settings of the blade feathering mechanisms on their machines. The results show that the BPMS was successful in recording the behaviour of the blade feathering mechanism in field trials with a 20 kW and a 30 kW wind turbine. The BPMS displays significant potential as an effective, inexpensive system for small wind turbine manufacturers to ensure the reliability of their pitch regulating over-speed protection mechanisms

warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

The wind energy industry has developed considerably in recent years with regard to large scale wind turbines. However, the small wind turbines (SWTs) are still underdeveloped. The classification of SWTs comes under the standard IEC6140001-2. When a small wind turbine is installed in an urban environment, it is exposed to complex environmental conditions, where high “surface roughness” in urban terrain due to buildings, street furniture and various obstacles causes a highly turbulent wind. This results in fatigue developing in turbine structures and poor performance. Turbulence is therefore a very important factor in small wind turbine functioning. But, in standards, turbulence intensity is considered a constant value for all wind classes for small wind turbines.



To assess the validity of the standard normal turbulence model (NTM) for SWTs for all sites, data from an open space and an urban area are analysed and compared. The data were collected from Ostergarnsholm Island in Sweden, as the open space, and the rooftop of a Bunnings warehouse in Port Kennedy as the urban area. The results for these two areas are compared with the standard NTM.



The outcome of the comparative analysis is that the rooftop areas are subject to greater turbulence intensity than that prescribed in the standard, and the open space turbulence intensity, on the other hand, is lower than the standard. Therefore, wider investigation and research are required in order to revise and improve the standard wind classes for small wind turbines

Reliability in performance is a key factor in ensuring the sustainable operation of a small wind turbine. Despite the great potential of small wind turbines to provide electric power, particularly in remote areas, many small wind turbines have short lifetimes due to technical failures or the excessive costs of numerous maintenance visits. In developing countries where the support infrastructure for wind turbine operation and maintenance has yet to be established, turbine reliability has a higher priority than efficiency of the turbine or, to quote from Schläpfer, “10% efficiency of something is always better than 80% efficiency of nothing”.



For wind turbines to be reliable they must have in place good mechanisms to protect themselves against very high winds or sudden removal of load. Both these scenarios can lead to “over-speeding” of the turbine rotor where the rotor experiences speed excursions that exceed the rated speed of the blade manufacturer. Over-speeding can lead to blade collapse with the possibility of damage to other turbine components and people and structures in the vicinity. For small horizontal-axis wind turbines (typically in the size range 0.1 – 30 kW), passive or mechanical protection systems are often used.  One common protection method is that of blade feathering where the turbine reacts to very high rotor speeds by reducing the pitch of its blades, thus regulating rotor speed by reducing the aerodynamic torque on the rotor.

Wind turbine blades are the most critical components of wind turbines. Full-scale blade fatigue testing is required to verify that the blades possess the strength and service life specified in the design. Unfortunately, the test must be run for a long time period. This problem led the blade testing laboratories to accelerate fatigue testing time. To achieve the objective, this thesis proposes two novel methods called STFT- and WT-based fatigue damage part extracting methods which are based on short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and wavelet transform (WT), respectively. For WT, different wavelet functions which are Morl, Meyr, Dmey, Mexh and DB30 are studied.



An aerodynamic computer code, HAWTsimulator, based on blade element momentum theory has been developed. This code is used to generate the sets of aerodynamic loads acting along the span of a ‘SERI-8 wind turbine blade’ in the range of wind speed from cut-in to cut-out. SERI-8 blades are installed on 65 kW wind turbines. Each set of aerodynamic loads is applied on the finite element model of the SERI-8 blade in structural software (ANSYS) to generate a plot of von Mises stress at the critical point on the blade versus wind speed. By relating this relationship to the wind speed data, the stress-time history at the critical point on the SERI-8 blade can be generated. It has the same sampling rate and length as the wind speed data.



A concept of applying accumulative power spectral density (AccPSD) distribution with time to identify fatigue damage events contained in the stress-time history has been introduced in this thesis. For STFT, AccPSD is the sum of power spectral density (PSD) of each frequency band at each time interval in the spectrogram. For WT, AccPSD is the sum of PSD of wavelet coefficients of each scale at each time interval in the scalogram. It is important that the blade feathering mechanism of a small wind turbine is tested before the turbine is installed in the field. This paper presents a simple system for monitoring the blade feathering of a turbine with an overall component cost that small wind turbine manufacturers can afford. The Blade Pitch Measurement System (BPMS) has been designed and constructed by the Research Institute of Sustainable Energy (RISE) and aids small wind turbine manufacturers in testing and optimising the settings of the blade feathering mechanisms on their machines. The results show that the BPMS was successful in recording the behaviour of the blade feathering mechanism in field trials with a 20 kW and a 30 kW wind turbine. The BPMS displays significant potential as an effective, inexpensive system for small wind turbine manufacturers to ensure the reliability of their pitch regulating over-speed protection mechanisms
